content: The journal provides specific instructions to authors regarding the topics suitable for submission and the types of papers accepted, such as original articles, reviews, or case reports. Additionally, the journal outlines unique requirements, including the number of manuscript copies needed, acceptable languages, article length, and approved abbreviations. Journals participating in international standards (over 500 globally) are expected to state in their author instructions that their requirements align with the Uniform Requirements for Manuscripts Submitted to Biomedical Journals and cite a published version of these guidelines. Manuscripts should be typed or printed on white bond paper, either 216 × 279 mm or ISO A4 (212 × 297 mm), with margins of at least 25 mm. Text should be double-spaced throughout, including the title page, abstract, main text, acknowledgments, references, tables, and figure legends. Pages must be numbered consecutively, starting with the title page, and the page number should be placed in the upper or lower right-hand corner. Each section or component of the manuscript should begin on a new page. Illustrations and unmounted prints should not exceed 203 × 254 mm. Authors are advised to submit the required number of paper copies and retain copies of all submitted materials. The title page must include the following: A concise yet informative title of the article. The name of each author, along with their highest academic degree(s) and institutional affiliation. The name of the department(s) and institution(s) to which the work should be attributed. Any disclaimers, if applicable. The name and address of the corresponding author responsible for manuscript-related correspondence. The name and address of the author to whom reprint requests should be addressed, or a statement indicating that reprints will not be available. Sources of support, such as grants, equipment, or drugs. A short running head or footline of no more than 40 characters (including letters and spaces) at the bottom of the title page. An increasing number of journals require electronic submission of manuscripts, either on a disk, as an email attachment, or via direct upload to the journal's website. Electronic submissions save time and postage costs and allow the manuscript to be handled electronically throughout the editorial process, including peer review. Authors can track the progress of their submission through the journal's website. Authors should consult the journal's instructions for acceptable word processing formats, file naming conventions, and other details. When submitting manuscripts, journals often require authors to provide an electronic copy (on a disk) when the paper is close to final acceptance. The disk should be clearly labeled with the file format and file name. Manuscripts should be sent in a sturdy envelope, with copies and figures protected by cardboard if necessary, to prevent damage to photographs. Photographs and transparencies should be placed in a separate sturdy envelope. Manuscripts must be accompanied by a cover letter signed by all co-authors, which should include: Information on prior or duplicate publication or submission elsewhere of any part of the work. A statement of financial or other relationships that could lead to a conflict of interest. A declaration that the manuscript has been read and approved by all authors, that authorship requirements have been met, and that each author believes the manuscript represents honest work. The name, address, and telephone number of the corresponding author responsible for communicating with co-authors about revisions and final proof approval. The cover letter should also provide any additional information that may assist the editor, such as the type of article the manuscript represents and whether the authors are willing to cover the cost of color illustrations. Copies of permissions to reproduce published material, use illustrations, report identifiable patient information, or name individuals for their contributions must accompany the manuscript. A copyright transfer may be required at this stage or after the paper is accepted for publication. Acknowledgment of manuscript receipt is typically received within 2–3 weeks, and a decision regarding publication is usually made within 6–8 weeks, depending on reviewers' responses. Rejection rates for top journals exceed 50%, and only about 5% of papers are accepted without changes recommended by peer review. Reviewers may suggest revisions to improve the paper's acceptability. Authors are not obligated to make all suggested changes but should address reviewers' criticisms where possible and justify any decisions not to do so. It is helpful to include a separate page indicating the criticisms made and how the revised paper responds to them, facilitating the editor's decision. Authorship in scientific papers is defined as substantial intellectual contribution to the study. According to the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors, authorship credit should be based on significant contributions to: 1. Conception and design, data acquisition, or data analysis and interpretation. 2. Drafting the article or revising it critically for important intellectual content. 3. Final approval of the version to be published. Authors must meet all three conditions. Acquisition of funding, data collection, or general supervision of the research group does not justify authorship. Journals may require authors to specify their contributions and those of individuals acknowledged but not listed as authors. Contributors must decide their level of contribution and whether it merits authorship. Authors listed in the byline should be ordered based on their actual contributions, as agreed upon by the authors. Contributors who do not meet authorship criteria should be acknowledged. All individuals listed must provide written permission to be acknowledged. There is increasing awareness of intellectual property rights among academics and scientific institutions. Sponsors of studies have the right to review manuscripts for a defined period (e.g., 30–60 days) before publication to allow for additional patent filings if needed. However, sponsors must not impede the subsequent publication of the study's full results. Researchers must receive credit for their work, and no one should be credited without active participation. All authors must agree to have their names on the paper and take public responsibility for it. The order of authors should be mutually agreed upon. Previous investigators' work on the topic should be cited, and credit should not be claimed for ideas already proposed or studied by others. Contributions of others who assisted in the research should be acknowledged, and the source of research support should be identified. Copyright must be respected. Copyright begins when a creative work is recorded in tangible form. In scholarly work, financial compensation for copyright is rare, but recognition is essential. No material from previously published work should be included without written permission from the publisher and author, and full credit to the source must be provided. Plagiarism, the use of another's words or ideas without acknowledgment, is a serious ethical offense. Conflicts of interest must be disclosed. Many journals require a conflict of interest statement before considering a paper for publication. Financial and funding ties can potentially distort research outcomes. Studies have shown that clinical trials supported by for-profit organizations are more likely to report favorable conclusions for the intervention. Redundant or duplicate publication, where a paper overlaps substantially with one already published by the same authors, is not acceptable unless explicitly stated. Journals generally do not accept papers that have been largely reported elsewhere. Authors must disclose all submissions and previous reports that might be considered redundant or duplicate. If redundancy is attempted or occurs without notification, editorial action, including rejection, can be expected. If the violation is discovered post-publication, a notice of redundant or duplicate publication may be issued. Secondary publication in another language or country is acceptable if specific conditions are met, including approval from both journals' editors, respect for the primary publication's priority, and clear acknowledgment of the primary reference. Patients' rights to privacy must be protected. Identifiable information should not be published without informed consent, which requires that patients have the right to review the manuscript. Identifying details should be omitted unless essential, and patient data should never be altered to achieve anonymity. Informed consent should be obtained if there is any doubt about anonymity. Researchers should seek recognition primarily among their peers. It is unethical to release findings to the public or media before communicating them to peers through scientific press or meetings.
